assignments.title: 23.7 Primary Source Exercise: Two Statements of 1945
assignments.html:
PRIMARY SOURCE EXERCISE
Two Statements of 1945
Truman on Hiroshima and Jackson at Nuremberg, in their own words.
Exercise · 16 points · Canvas text entry
⚖ ─ ⚖ ─ ⚖
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then write your answers and submit them as the submission box below describes.
THE TASK

Read these two short passages again in their primary source pages. Truman, August 6, 1945: “Sixteen hours ago an American airplane dropped one bomb on Hiroshima, an important Japanese Army base.” Jackson, November 21, 1945: “That four great nations, flushed with victory and stung with injury stay the hand of vengeance and voluntarily submit their captive enemies to the judgment of the law is one of the most significant tributes that Power has ever paid to Reason.”

Answer the four questions below in the Canvas text box. Aim for four to six sentences each. You will be graded on the quality of your argument, not on which answer you give.

QUESTIONS

1. Truman calls Hiroshima “an important Japanese Army base.” “Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and Truman's Choice” says it was a city of about 350,000 people that held an army headquarters. What does the statement say about the power of the bomb, and what does it leave out about the people of the city? What does an official statement gain by choosing its words this way?

2. Truman ties the bomb to Pearl Harbor and to the Potsdam ultimatum. Use “Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and Truman's Choice” to explain what the Potsdam Declaration demanded and what it did not say about the emperor. Then name one fact the statement does not mention that a historian would want to know before judging the decision.

3. Jackson says the winners chose “the judgment of the law” over vengeance. Use “Nuremberg and the United Nations” to name one objection to the trial, such as “ex post facto” law or victors’ justice, and say how the court answered it. Does the objection still have some force? Explain.

4. Choose ONE. (a) Suppose that before Potsdam Truman had told Japan it could keep its emperor. (b) Suppose the Allies had shot the Nazi leaders without a trial, as Churchill at one time favored. Explain how events might have gone differently, and what evidence from the lessons supports your guess. Then say what makes your guess uncertain.

GRADING RUBRIC (16 pts)
CriteriaExcellent (4)Proficient (3)Developing (2)Beginning (1)

MODULE INTRODUCTION
Module Introduction: Victory and Its Judgment
Survey · 3 questions · not graded
⚖ ─ ⚖ ─ ⚖
Before you start

Welcome to Victory and Its Judgment. Answer the questions below before you open the first lesson. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting. This survey is not graded.

This module's goals:
  • Explain how the atomic bomb was built and how Truman came to decide to use it.
  • State the main arguments historians make about the decision.
  • Describe the Nuremberg trial, the objections to it, and the founding of the United Nations.

discussions.title: 23.8 Discussion: Was Truman right to use the atomic bomb?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
Was Truman right to use the atomic bomb?
A question on which thoughtful people still disagree.
Graded discussion · 10 points · one post and one reply
⚖ ─ ⚖ ─ ⚖
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then post your answer to the prompt below, and reply to one classmate.
DISCUSSION PROMPT

This week’s question: Was Truman right to use the atomic bomb?

This is a question on which thoughtful people still disagree. Choose a side. Name the strongest fact from “Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and Truman's Choice” for your side and the strongest fact for the other side, then say why yours is stronger. Say also which moral rule about a commander’s duty your answer depends on.

Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a fact or decision they did not use. If not, say politely where you think it falls short, and give your reason.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
CriteriaSubstantive (full credit)Thin (partial credit)Missing (no credit)
Your claim and your reasons
